short: The joint monarchs installed by the Glorious Revolution on Parliament's terms.
full:
James II's Catholic policies and the birth of a Catholic heir in June 1688 prompted seven English notables to invite his daughter Mary and her husband William of Orange to intervene. William landed at Torbay in November; James's army disintegrated without a battle and he fled to France. The Convention Parliament declared the throne vacant and in February 1689 offered it jointly to William and Mary, together with the Declaration of Rights.

The Bill of Rights that followed barred Catholics from the throne, banned a standing army in peacetime and taxation without parliamentary consent, and required frequent parliaments; the Toleration Act granted freedom of worship to Protestant dissenters. In Scotland and Ireland the change was fought over, at Killiecrankie and then the Boyne in 1690. William's real interest was the continental war against Louis XIV, funded from 1694 by the new Bank of England. Mary died of smallpox that year, and William ruled alone until a riding accident killed him in 1702.
